note: Telescope, globe and microscope content for the apartment. Globe maps are equirectangular, longitude -180 at the left edge and 0 in the middle, north up. sky: ra/dec are J2000 degrees (planets, moon and sun have none: compute them); fov_deg is roughly the angular width the picture spans. All images are public domain or CC0; per-file sources and licences are in data/full/scope-sources.json.

globes.name: EARTH
globes.credit: NASA Earth Observatory (Blue Marble: Next Generation, Reto Stöckli); night lights: NASA Earth Observatory / Suomi NPP (Black Marble 2012)

globes.name: THE MOON
globes.credit: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, CGI Moon Kit (LRO / LROC WAC colour)

globes.name: MARS
globes.credit: NASA / JPL / USGS, Viking MDIM 2.1 colourised global mosaic

sky.name: THE SUN
sky.about: Seen through a safe solar filter, the dark sunspots are storms bigger than the whole Earth.
sky.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - Global Science and Technology, Inc./Tom Bridgman, eMITS/Joy Ng, ADNET Systems, Inc./Laurence Schuler, ADNET Systems, In

sky.name: THE MOON
sky.about: The dark patches are old lava plains, and every bright dot is a crater from something that hit it.

sky.name: MERCURY
sky.about: The smallest planet, baked on one side and frozen on the other, cratered just like our Moon.
sky.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Arizona State University/Carnegie Institution of Washington

sky.name: VENUS
sky.about: The brightest planet in the sky, wrapped in clouds of acid so thick you never see the ground.

sky.name: MARS
sky.about: The red planet; that long scar across it is a canyon that would stretch from New York to Los Angeles.

sky.name: JUPITER
sky.about: The biggest planet; the red spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries.
sky.credit: NASA, ESA, and A. Simon (NASA Goddard), edited by PlanetUser

sky.name: SATURN
sky.about: Its rings are billions of chunks of ice, some as small as a grain of sand, some as big as a house.

sky.name: URANUS
sky.about: An ice giant tipped on its side, so it rolls around the Sun like a ball.

sky.name: NEPTUNE
sky.about: The farthest planet, with the fastest winds in the solar system.

sky.name: ORION NEBULA
sky.about: A cloud of glowing gas in Orion's sword where new stars are being born right now.
sky.credit: NASA, ESA, M. Robberto (Space Telescope Science Institute/ESA) and the Hubble Space Telescope Orion Treasury Project Team

sky.name: ANDROMEDA GALAXY
sky.about: The farthest thing you can see with the naked eye: a trillion stars, 2.5 million light-years away.

sky.name: PLEIADES
sky.about: The Seven Sisters, a family of young blue stars still wrapped in a wisp of dust.

sky.name: CRAB NEBULA
sky.about: What is left of a star that exploded in the year 1054, bright enough then to see in daylight.
sky.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University)

sky.name: RING NEBULA
sky.about: A dying star puffed off its outer layers into a glowing smoke ring.

sky.name: WHIRLPOOL GALAXY
sky.about: A spiral galaxy tugging on a smaller neighbour that is passing right by it.

sky.name: SOMBRERO GALAXY
sky.about: A galaxy seen almost edge-on, with a dark lane of dust around it like the brim of a hat.
sky.credit: NASA/ESA and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

sky.name: PILLARS OF CREATION
sky.about: Towers of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, each one taller than our whole solar system.
sky.credit: Credit: NASA, Jeff Hester, and Paul Scowen (Arizona State University)

sky.name: LAGOON NEBULA
sky.about: The heart of the Lagoon, where hot young stars carve twisting shapes into the gas.

sky.name: HERCULES CLUSTER
sky.about: Hundreds of thousands of ancient stars packed into a ball, older than almost anything in our galaxy.
sky.credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

sky.name: DUMBBELL NEBULA
sky.about: The glowing shell of a dying star, shaped a bit like an apple core.

sky.name: TRIANGULUM GALAXY
sky.about: The middle of our third-biggest neighbour galaxy, packed with dust lanes and young blue stars.
sky.credit: , , and M. Durbin, J. Dalcanton, and B.F. Williams (University of Washington)

slides.name: A FLEA
slides.about: Robert Hooke drew this flea in 1665, one of the first close-ups of a bug anyone had ever seen.

slides.name: A FLEA, UP CLOSE
slides.about: The same kind of flea under an electron microscope, flattened so it can slip between hairs.

slides.name: CORK
slides.about: Hooke looked at a slice of cork, saw tiny boxes and called them cells, the word we still use.

slides.name: A SNOWFLAKE
slides.about: Wilson Bentley photographed over 5,000 snowflakes and never found two alike.

slides.name: SNOW CRYSTAL
slides.about: A real snow crystal, frozen and scanned in an electron microscope.
slides.credit: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Electron and Confocal Microscopy Laboratory

slides.name: RADIOLARIANS
slides.about: Single-celled sea creatures that build glass skeletons like tiny chandeliers.

slides.name: DIATOMS
slides.about: Algae in glass shells; they make about a fifth of the oxygen you breathe.
slides.credit: Prof. Gordon T. Taylor, Stony Brook University (NOAA Corps Collection)

slides.name: A DIATOM
slides.about: One diatom, its glass shell patterned like a stained-glass window.

slides.name: POLLEN
slides.about: Pollen from different flowers: spiky, smooth and bean-shaped, each kind its own shape.

slides.name: MUSHROOM SPORES
slides.about: The underside of a button mushroom, covered in spores waiting for the wind.

slides.name: LEAF SKIN
slides.about: The skin of a leaf, with tiny hairs sticking up from it.
slides.credit: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility

slides.name: AN APHID
slides.about: A greenfly, the little bug that sucks the sap out of garden plants.
slides.credit: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility

slides.name: GRASSHOPPER HEAD
slides.about: The face of a grasshopper: big eyes, feelers and jaws made for chewing leaves.
slides.credit: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility

slides.name: A WEEVIL
slides.about: A beetle with a long snout, the pest that gets into old flour and rice.
slides.credit: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility

slides.name: FIREFLY FACE
slides.about: A firefly up close; the light comes from its tail, not its face.
slides.credit: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility

slides.name: A FLY'S EYE
slides.about: A fruit fly's eye is hundreds of tiny eyes packed together, with bristles in between.
slides.credit: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth College Electron Microscope Facility

slides.name: A BEDBUG
slides.about: A bedbug's mouth folded under its head: check the old mattresses before you buy one.

slides.name: A PLANT MITE
slides.about: A mite smaller than the dot on this i, living on the leaves of fruit trees.
slides.credit: USDA ARS: Eric Erbe, colourised by Chris Pooley

slides.name: A MITE ON A BEE
slides.about: A varroa mite riding on a honeybee, hidden among its hairs.
slides.credit: USDA ARS: Eric Erbe, Christopher Pooley

slides.name: BUTTERFLY WING
slides.about: Butterfly wings are tiled with tiny coloured scales, like shingles on a roof.

slides.name: A WATER BEAR
slides.about: The first drawing of a tardigrade, from 1773: a tiny beast that can survive outer space.

slides.name: AN AMOEBA
slides.about: A blob that moves by pouring itself forward and swallows its food whole.
slides.credit: Joseph Leidy, Fresh-water Rhizopods of North America (1879)

slides.name: VOLVOX
slides.about: A rolling green ball of thousands of cells that swim together, with baby balls inside.

slides.name: ONION SKIN
slides.about: Onion skin cells lined up like bricks in a wall.
slides.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library (CC0)

slides.name: A CHEEK CELL
slides.about: A cell scraped from the inside of a cheek, the dark dot is its nucleus.

slides.name: BLOOD CELLS
slides.about: A red blood cell, a platelet and a white blood cell, the three things floating in your blood.

slides.name: BACTERIA
slides.about: E. coli, rod-shaped bacteria that live in your gut by the billions.

slides.name: PENICILLIUM MOLD
slides.about: The mold on old bread and oranges; one kind gave us penicillin.

slides.name: YEAST
slides.about: The tiny fungus that makes bread rise, here budding off new cells.

slides.name: BLACK SAND
slides.about: Black sand from a Hawaiian beach, made of lava that shattered when it hit the sea.

slides.name: A HUMAN HAIR
slides.about: A single hair, covered in overlapping scales like a pine cone.

slides.name: FISH SCALES
slides.about: Zebrafish scales overlapping like roof tiles, lit up with coloured dyes.

paramecium.about: Paramecium (also Paramoecium) is a genus of unicellular ciliates, commonly studied as a representative of the ciliate group. Paramecia are widespread in freshwater, brackish, and marine environments and are often very abundant in stagnant basins and ponds.

euglena.about: Euglena is a genus of single-celled flagellate eukaryotes. It is the best known and most widely studied member of the class Euglenoidea, a diverse group containing some 54 genera and at least 800 species. Species of Euglena are found in fresh and salt waters.

amoeba.about: Amoeba, alternatively Chaos diffluens, is an amoeba closely related to the giant amoebae and a species commonly bought at science supply stores.

rotifer.about: The rotifers (Rotifera, commonly called wheel animals) make up a phylum of microscopic and near-microscopic pseudocoelomate animals.

volvox.about: Volvox is a polyphyletic genus of chlorophyte green algae in the family Volvocaceae. It forms spherical colonies of up to 50,000 cells. They live in a variety of freshwater habitats, and were first reported by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in 1700.

diatom.about: Diatoms are a major group of microalgae, and are among the most common types of phytoplankton.

daphnia.about: Daphnia, a genus of small planktonic crustaceans, are 0.2–5 millimetres (0.01–0.20 in) in length.

tardigrade.about: Tardigrades are water-dwelling, eight-legged, segmented micro-animals. They were first discovered by the German zoologist Johann August Ephraim Goeze in 1773.
